DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

**Overall:** The case for a price rise is reasonable, but the paper is not "low-risk and well evidenced" as written. It contains one factual error that drives a recommendation, and it leaves out a cost change that its own supplier section reports. I would not approve it as it stands.

## What checks out
- The table's margins match its prices and costs, and plates sum to 1,050.
- £810/week is correct on its stated assumptions (310 + 260 + 240), and £42,120 is 52 × £810.
- All three proposed prices are below the competitor range midpoints (£17.975, £16.50, £29.50).

## Main problems

**1. The risotto rationale is wrong.** Section 5.2 says risotto has "the weakest margin on the menu." Table 1 shows the opposite: at 80% it has the *highest* margin, and steak (60%) has the lowest. It does have the lowest sales of the named dishes, at 90 plates, but that is the same as the aggregated specials line. At £11.20 gross profit per plate, risotto earns about £1,000/week. If the replacement special performs like your other specials (64% margin), you lose about £2.25 a plate, roughly **£200/week or £10k/year**. The proposal needs the expected cost and margin of the replacement. It also needs to say whether risotto is your only vegetarian main, since dropping it would then be a menu-coverage issue as well.

**2. The beef cost rise is ignored in the projection.** Section 4 reports a 12% beef increase from 1 April, but 5.3 uses today's food costs.
- Steak: about +£1.25 per plate, so the £2 increase nets only about £0.75. At £28 the margin would be about 58%, *below* today's 60%.
- Burger: +£0.25 to £0.50 per plate, depending on how much of the £4.20 is beef.
- That is roughly **£215–280/week** of added cost. Together with the risotto point, the headline gain falls from about £42k to something nearer **£17–21k/year** before any volume loss.
- The "about 71%" main-course margin only holds on unchanged costs. By my rough estimate (assuming specials average about £18), it falls to about 69% once beef is included, little better than today. The paper should show this calculation.

**3. "Volumes will hold" is asserted, not evidenced.**
- Break-even is tight. Fish and chips loses money on the change if volume falls by about 8% (about 25 plates). Steak, once beef is included, breaks even at roughly a 5% fall.
- A 60% repeat share shows loyalty, but repeat guests are the ones most likely to notice a rise, and the figure is a share of bookings, not of covers or spend.
- The claim that the 2024 change had "no visible effect" gives no size for that increase and no data, and conditions have changed since.
- The claim that weekday lunch is a "small share" of mains has no figure behind it.

**4. The data base is thinner than described.**
- January–February is a single winter period, so annualizing it to 52 weeks assumes spring and summer volumes are similar.
- The "full competitor check" covers five restaurants and three dishes. Curry and risotto were not compared.
- After the increases, your fish and chips (£17.50) would no longer be the lowest in the group. Competitors also face the beef rise and may raise prices themselves, which would help you, but that is speculation either way.

**5. The monitoring plan is weak.** Menus are reprinted before any signal arrives, so eight weeks of tracking is not an "early warning." There are no trigger thresholds or fallback. Comparing April–May with a January–February baseline is also confounded by seasonality. Define what a problem looks like (for example, fish and chips down more than 5% for three weeks) and what you would do about it.

## Smaller points
- Section 8 says "six trading days a week," but section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five.
- The "70% overall target" is for all courses, while the 71% figure is for mains only, so they are not directly comparable.
- The paper sets no explicit margin target per dish, which would make the steak problem obvious.

## Suggested revisions before approval
1. Correct the risotto statement and either justify removal with the replacement's costed margin or keep risotto.
2. Rebuild the projection with post-April costs, and show base, and downside cases (for example, −5% and −10% volume).
3. Consider a larger steak increase or a smaller beef-heavy portion, since £28 does not restore its margin.
4. Add monitoring thresholds and a review date.

Note that the document is dated March 2026 and it's now November. If these changes went ahead, comparing actual till data since April with these projections would be more useful than the forecast.
